forest_02_001.speaker: narrator
forest_02_001.text: By Yue's third morning in the village, the apprentice room smelled of everyone's boots. Someone had hung a string above the stove for drying socks, and the lowest pair dripped onto the kindling. Wen Cai's sister came to take the laundry basket, inspected the string and moved it with the authority of someone tired of solving that particular problem. She left Yue's dry socks where they were and carried off the wet ones without asking whose feet had made them troublesome.

forest_02_002.speaker: narrator
forest_02_002.text: Outside, frost whitened the fence rails. Wen Cai waited with two ordinary work aprons and a parcel of bread. He offered Yue the cleaner apron; she picked the one without a torn pocket. He looked at the pocket as though seeing it for the first time. 'That is where the charcoal tries to escape,' he said. She put on the sound apron and asked where they were going. He pointed toward the banked kilns beyond the upper lane.

forest_02_003.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_003.text: 'You can spend today learning what a dry bag means,' he said. 'Every buyer pronounces the words as though the weather has signed them.' He handed her half the bread. 'My sister says you will forget to eat because the smoke looks interesting. I said nobody could find that smoke interesting for long. She told me to bring bread anyway.' Yue ate while they walked, pleased to be anticipated for an ordinary failing.

forest_02_004.speaker: narrator
forest_02_004.text: The kiln yard lay against a slope sheltered from the sharpest wind. A low roof kept rain off the finished charcoal store. Behind it, stacks of billets waited under covers raised clear of the wet ground. Yue's first impression was of patient order. Then she saw that one cover had blown loose, wetting the ends of a stack marked for tomorrow. A worker was trying to conceal the darker wood by turning its cut faces inward.

forest_02_005.speaker: narrator
forest_02_005.text: Wen Cai took the worker aside before Yue could ask a public question. The man was his uncle, grey-haired and broad-handed, with a habit of grinding his jaw when cornered. They spoke too quietly for her to hear. The uncle finally untied the stack mark and went to tell the keeper about the rain. Wen Cai stood beside the wet billets for a moment after he left. The clean apron had become suddenly irrelevant.

forest_02_006.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_006.text: 'He thinks I invite visitors to shame him,' Wen said when Yue approached. 'He has spent thirty years trying to get a day's wood dry before somebody changes the day's order.' Yue asked whether the rain had ruined the stack. 'No. It has delayed it. Sometimes delay feels worse because everyone can still see the thing you were supposed to deliver.' He retied the cover at the loose corner and tested the new knot.

forest_02_007.speaker: narrator
forest_02_007.text: The keeper assigned Yue to the finished store with a worker who could read the moisture checks. They weighed a sample, broke it to inspect the interior and set a second sample in the approved drying space. The process took time. A cool dark surface could hide dampness that changed a sack's weight. Yue's hands came away black from the first piece. She rubbed her thumb against the apron, leaving a broad mark directly beneath the clean pocket.

forest_02_008.speaker: narrator
forest_02_008.text: A girl sorting fragments nearby grinned at the mark and offered a basin. The basin's water was already grey. Yue held her hands above it, uncertain how much cleaner they could become. The girl showed her the rough washing cloth hung beside it, then said she should stop aiming for festival hands before work was finished. Yue laughed and washed only the grit that would rub her skin raw. Her hands remained recognizably employed.

forest_02_009.speaker: narrator
forest_02_009.text: Near midday, Long Qian's clerk came for the first sacks. He pressed one with his palm, declared it dry, and asked the crew to hurry. The keeper said the interior sample had not completed its check. The clerk watched the testing shelf with visible annoyance. The fragments on Yue's table looked suddenly like the cause of a stopped road. She continued sorting at the keeper's pace, though the clerk's silence made her fingers clumsy.

forest_02_010.speaker: narrator
forest_02_010.text: Wen Cai's uncle brought over the bread parcel's remaining crust and set it beside Yue's hand. 'Black bread, black hands,' he said. 'Nobody can see which one you dropped.' It was his first direct attempt at friendliness. She ate the crust without brushing away the coal dust, then regretted it at once. The uncle laughed hard enough to cough. He fetched clean water and looked less like a man being judged while she rinsed her mouth.

forest_02_011.speaker: long_qian
forest_02_011.text: Long Qian arrived before the clerk lost his temper. 'I need the dry sacks,' he said after seeing the unfinished checks. 'How late will they be?' The keeper gave an actual interval. Long went to the waiting driver, changed the departure notice and paid for the additional standing time. When he returned, the clerk complained about the expense. 'You would prefer to buy water at charcoal prices,' Long answered. 'The kitchen still has to burn it afterward.'

forest_02_012.speaker: narrator
forest_02_012.text: The corrected sacks left in the afternoon, lighter than the clerk's first quick figure. Long Qian stood watching them until the cart cleared the turn. He had defended the drying check because bad fuel would harm his kitchen orders. That same concern would soon make him argue for more forest cutting. Yue found the connection unsettling. Good conduct in the store did not tell her what price he would ask someone else to pay when the next shortage reached him.

forest_02_013.speaker: narrator
forest_02_013.text: At the cooling kiln, the keeper invited her to watch a scheduled opening from behind its marked distance. The door's first crack released a breath of bitter hot air. Workers used long tools to pull the charcoal into a covered, nonflammable receiving space. One glowing fragment looked asleep beneath grey ash until it touched a dry splinter. A flame jumped up, bright and quick. The keeper smothered it before it crossed the receiving tray.

forest_02_014.speaker: narrator
forest_02_014.text: Yue felt the heat against her cheeks although she stood beyond the working line. Her first instinct was to bring qi into the hand nearest her blade. The kiln's problem would not be solved by a reinforced sword movement. She let the impulse pass and watched the keeper inspect the tray. The girl from the sorting table tapped her own empty glove, reminding Yue where her hands should remain. Neither apprentice needed to be impressive beside the open door.

forest_02_015.speaker: shi_lan
forest_02_015.text: 'This is why I do not call every flame a burn,' Shi Lan said when she arrived for the afternoon check. 'The kiln is controlling an enclosed process. The hillside crew works with moving air, dead litter and a different escape problem. A good kiln worker can be new to a field fire. A good field warden can spoil a charcoal batch.' She nodded toward the keeper. 'He has accused me of exactly that before.'

forest_02_016.speaker: narrator
forest_02_016.text: The keeper said her spoiled batch was famous chiefly because she had tried to label it a research result. Shi Lan accepted the accusation with a grin that changed her entire face. Wen Cai's uncle supplied the missing detail: she had dropped the experimental tray while avoiding a bee. The apprentices laughed. Yue could suddenly imagine the warden younger and less severe, standing in the same yard with scattered charcoal and a very small enemy.

forest_02_017.speaker: shi_lan
forest_02_017.text: 'The bee had a sound escape plan,' she said. 'I did not. You may learn from both of us.' She took the afternoon measurements from the keeper and went through them without a ceremonial change of voice. The joke did not make her less attentive. Yue watched how quickly the workers returned to ordinary tasks after laughter, as if it had loosened their shoulders rather than given them permission to ignore the heat.

forest_02_018.speaker: narrator
forest_02_018.text: When the yard closed its apprentice tasks, Wen Cai took Yue along a path above the stacks. The lower village roofs looked close enough to warm from the kiln smoke, though the air reaching them was already cold. He pointed out his sister's future house, its unfinished roof covered in reed mats. A basin stood inside to catch leaks. The couple had bought a good door before learning what the ridge timber would cost.

forest_02_019.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_019.text: 'She wanted a door that shuts without lifting it,' he said. 'That seemed modest enough.' Yue asked whether the carpenter could finish the roof with a different wood. 'Yes. The lighter wood needs a closer support spacing. More work, less timber cost. They are asking whether they can trade their own labour for part of it.' His voice grew careful. 'I do not want you to solve that for us. I would like you to see the house before anyone calls the delay greed.'

forest_02_020.speaker: narrator
forest_02_020.text: They walked down to the house. Wen Cai's sister was fitting cloth over the basin to stop roof grit falling into the collected rain. Her intended husband sat on a stool making pegs. Both greeted Yue with the embarrassed hospitality of people whose new home was still too unfinished to shelter a visitor. She admired the door when they showed it to her. It closed with a quiet, satisfying click, exactly as the sister had wanted.

forest_02_021.speaker: narrator
forest_02_021.text: Yue left after sharing a piece of roasted turnip beside the door. The house's basin, pegs and reed roof stayed with her more firmly than its debt terms. She had once wanted strength so that useful things would stop waiting on other people's decisions. Here strength could hold a beam while the carpenter set it. It could not shorten the season of wood, buy the family's work twice, or make them accept a visitor's idea of the home they should want.

forest_02_022.speaker: narrator
forest_02_022.text: The first snow fell that evening in small hard grains, scarcely enough to whiten the alley. Shi Lan's niece tried to catch them on her tongue and complained that winter was being stingy. The warden told her to keep the scarf over her mouth anyway. Yue found the child's new mitten hanging beside the stove instead of on her hand. Returning it earned a solemn promise that it had only been removed to improve the catching.

forest_02_023.speaker: narrator
forest_02_023.text: At the lodging stove, Wen Cai's uncle sat rubbing a thumb swollen from an old split. He insisted the thumb always looked that way in cold weather. The keeper asked when it had become difficult to bend. Their voices grew louder until Shi Lan put a kettle on the stove and gave both men somewhere to look. The uncle finally agreed to visit the ordinary clinic after breakfast. He still wanted his evening drying task counted as finished.

forest_02_024.speaker: shi_lan
forest_02_024.text: 'Who assigned you evening drying?' Shi Lan asked. The uncle named a deputy keeper who had already gone home. She wrote the offered account in her work book and asked the lodging watch to check the yard before sleep. Nobody was punished in the stove room. Yue watched the uncle relax by a small amount when the question moved toward a named task rather than his presumed foolishness.

forest_02_025.speaker: narrator
forest_02_025.text: Long Qian visited the hall to discuss kitchen fuel with the cook. He found the cutters arguing over how many sacks could leave at dawn and took the argument to a separate table. Yue remained at the stove with the niece, who was drawing a fox's stolen boots in ash on a slate. The fox now had six boots and four feet. Its growing logistical trouble absorbed the child more fully than any buyer's speech could have done.

forest_02_026.speaker: narrator
forest_02_026.text: A shout came from the back yard while the niece was deciding where the extra boots should go. The lodging watch had found smoke under the drying shed's door. It was low and thick, unlike the thinner plume over a working kiln. Shi Lan rose at once. She handed the child to the cook, told Yue to fetch the outside lantern, and took the long latch hook from its marked place beside the stove.

forest_02_027.speaker: narrator
forest_02_027.text: At the shed, a worker was slumped against a stack of sacks near the inner wall. The watch had called to him and received no answer. Shi Lan barred the nearest apprentice from entering. She used the long hook to open the high outside shutter, then opened the door from its latch side. Air moved through the room. The ember tray beneath the sacks had burned poorly in the shut shed, making its atmosphere dangerous before anyone saw a flame.

forest_02_028.speaker: narrator
forest_02_028.text: The keeper and a rested worker stood at the door under Shi Lan's direction. They brought the slumped man into the open using a long board and pull strap placed from the ventilated approach; nobody was sent blindly into the thick interior air. Yue held the lantern high enough for them to see the sill. She wanted to help lift him by hand. Shi Lan's glance kept her on the task already making the extraction possible.

forest_02_029.speaker: narrator
forest_02_029.text: Outside, the man coughed and tried to sit up. Ren's visiting clinic assistant had been lodged near the yard and came with an ordinary treatment satchel. She kept him still, assessed his breathing and arranged the safe transfer to the clinic. Shi Lan's niece watched from the cook's doorway, suddenly silent. The cook brought the child inside before the rescue became another duty her small body had to perform by watching.

forest_02_030.speaker: narrator
forest_02_030.text: The ember tray was made safe by the qualified yard crew with the shed open and the adjacent stored fuel isolated. The keeper found that damp sacks had been placed too close to it and the high shutter tied shut against snow. He retained the tie before moving the remaining stock. Wen Cai's uncle arrived with his swollen thumb wrapped in cloth. He stared at the tie, then sat down without being asked.

forest_02_031.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_031.text: 'He was finishing my uncle's turn,' Wen Cai said beside the shed wall. 'I knew they were hurrying the sacks. I did not know about this tray.' His voice was flat with the effort of making it exact. Yue handed him the lantern when her arm tired. He held it without looking at the injured worker's empty place. The small exchange gave each of them a task while the larger knowledge kept changing.

forest_02_032.speaker: narrator
forest_02_032.text: The deputy keeper returned after a runner fetched him from home. He admitted instructing the crew to keep snow off the drying sacks but denied ordering an ember tray inside the closed shed. The uncle said the tray had been the deputy's usual shortcut last winter. Two workers described different earlier uses. Shi Lan kept the accounts separate and closed the shed to drying until the actual safe arrangement could be inspected. The timber order would have to wait through that closure.

forest_02_033.speaker: narrator
forest_02_033.text: Rong Sui came after hearing that his morning delivery might fail. At the closed shed he asked first how many sacks had been saved. Shi Lan answered with the clinic's receiving address. He understood the correction and went there. Yue saw his face on returning: pale, still controlled, with a line at the mouth that had not been present beside his careful ledger. He offered to fund the injured man's missed shift without a release of claims.

forest_02_034.speaker: rong_sui
forest_02_034.text: 'I need a receipt for the payment,' he said to the clerk. 'Not a sentence saying the accident is settled.' The clerk wrote the distinction. Shi Lan watched him sign. 'You should have begun with the man,' she said afterward. Rong kept the pen in his hand. 'Yes,' he answered. The single word did more than the explanation Yue had expected, and left the original question about delivery hanging where it belonged.

forest_02_035.speaker: narrator
forest_02_035.text: Before midnight, the injured worker was breathing more comfortably under ordinary clinic observation. He could not return to the yard the next morning. The uncle stayed outside the sickroom because the assistant asked for a quieter space. Wen Cai sat beside him on a bench, their shoulders close without touching. Yue brought each a hot cup. Nobody used the improved breathing to declare the closed drying method safe.

forest_02_036.speaker: narrator
forest_02_036.text: Back in the lodging room, Yue washed smoke from her face and found a small ash print on her sleeve. The niece had clutched it when the shout came. The child was asleep with both mittens beside her pillow. Shi Lan stood at the door and looked at the print for a long moment. Then she asked Yue whether she had eaten since the afternoon. The answer was no. The warden fetched the saved bread without another question.

forest_02_037.speaker: lin_yue
forest_02_037.text: 'I kept wanting to do something larger,' Yue said over the bread. Shi Lan leaned against the doorpost. 'You held the light where we needed it. I could see the pull strap.' Yue looked at the lantern, now cooling on its hook. She had wanted enough strength to stop being the person behind a line. Tonight the line had kept her useful, though accepting that usefulness still felt smaller than wanting it.

forest_02_038.speaker: shi_lan
forest_02_038.text: 'When my first fire went wrong, I ran toward the loudest voice,' Shi Lan said. 'I did not notice the quiet man beside the broken gate. He was the one who knew where the water barrel had fallen.' She spoke as if finishing a conversation with herself. 'Sometimes a task looks small because you are looking at it from the place where everybody is praising another task. Go to sleep. We need clear eyes tomorrow.'

forest_02_039.speaker: narrator
forest_02_039.text: In the morning, snow covered the yard's old footprints and left the shed tie hanging dark against a pale wall. The buyers met beside the closed door, both facing delayed deliveries from the same crews. Long Qian offered to send a kitchen worker to help inspect alternate covered storage. Rong Sui offered another cart for cleared dry sacks. Each help had a stated cost and use. Neither reopened the unsafe shed merely by making a useful offer.

forest_02_040.speaker: narrator
forest_02_040.text: The keeper moved cleared dry stock to the sound store under counted receiving marks. Damp sacks stayed separate for inspection. Long Qian's clerk tried to combine the two groups on his cart list and was stopped by the girl who sorted fragments. She pointed to the marks and said he could not cook with a combined figure. He corrected the list, then asked her how to read the store's new labels. She explained without lowering her voice.

forest_02_041.speaker: narrator
forest_02_041.text: Wen Cai's uncle asked the crew to cover his next turn because the clinic had told him to rest the thumb. He made the request in front of the same men who had heard him deny the injury. One laughed, then offered the morning hour. Another needed his own scheduled rest and declined. The foreman made a paid replacement from the crew's fund. The uncle looked embarrassed and relieved, both expressions visible without a tale about his toughness.

forest_02_042.speaker: narrator
forest_02_042.text: By supper, the delayed delivery had a new date, the unsafe shed had a physical lock, and two workers were off the yard on different medical limits. The wood still needed drying. Yue copied the final task list after the keeper checked it, then joined Wen Cai on the step outside. He watched snow settle on the little roof his sister wanted repaired. Their conversation began with her good door and ended, for once, without trying to put a price on it.

forest_02_043.speaker: narrator
forest_02_043.text: On the fourth day, the village grain house opened its shutters early. Long Qian had arranged a limited delivery before the next cold road check. Workers queued with purchase slips, while a second line received ordinary relief portions from the council's separate store. The distinction was visible in the sacks stacked behind each counter. Yue had come to help move the unloaded containers. She found Wen Cai's sister standing in the purchase line with a folded paper held tightly enough to crease its corners.

forest_02_044.speaker: narrator
forest_02_044.text: The sister had been offered grain on credit against future charcoal wages. She wanted to accept the grain and feared the term that directed all the household's charcoal through one buyer until repayment. Her intended husband had a small eastern turn under Rong Sui's contract. Long Qian's clerk said the new paper did not concern him because the household was not yet joined. The sister asked whether he would repeat that answer after the marriage. The clerk paused over his ink.

forest_02_045.speaker: long_qian
forest_02_045.text: 'It is a household pledge once the household signs,' Long Qian said when he joined them. 'I will not pretend it ends when the wedding begins.' Wen Cai's sister withdrew her paper from the counter. Long looked at the nearly empty basket in her hand. 'You can buy a smaller present quantity without that pledge.' She asked its cash price. It was still more than the money she had brought.

forest_02_046.speaker: narrator
forest_02_046.text: Yue stood with an empty transport sack folded over one arm and wanted to offer the difference. The sister noticed the movement toward her purse and shook her head before Yue reached it. She asked Long Qian whether she could pay part now and the balance from carpenter work already accepted by the council. He needed the actual work receipt before approving a limited advance. She went to fetch it, leaving the future-charcoal pledge unsigned.

forest_02_047.speaker: narrator
forest_02_047.text: When the sister returned, the receipt supported a smaller grain advance against defined paid carpenter hours. It did not bind her intended husband's eastern charcoal. Long Qian authorized that alternative at his ordinary service charge and wrote the amount on its own line. The sister accepted after reading it. Yue admired her persistence and disliked the charge. Those responses remained separate while she helped carry the purchased sack to the waiting cart.

forest_02_048.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_048.text: 'You look angry at him,' Wen Cai said after his sister left. Yue answered that the charge seemed hard on a household already waiting for a roof. 'It is,' he said. 'The grain arrived because his carts came. I can be thankful for the grain and angry about the pledge. My uncle thinks that is ingratitude. He likes choosing one feeling and staying with it.' Wen rolled the empty sack so tightly that Yue could see which feeling occupied him now.

forest_02_049.speaker: narrator
forest_02_049.text: The grain-house keeper asked them to move the relief stock before the purchase counter's next crowd arrived. Wen Cai worked fast, then slowed when an older woman asked for a sack to be lifted onto her low handcart. Yue followed her through the yard to check the wheel's clear route. The woman had come early to avoid standing in line on her knee. A familiar delay appeared in a different form: even grain already set aside could be hard to reach.

forest_02_050.speaker: narrator
forest_02_050.text: At the far counter, Rong Sui's runner was buying food for the eastern crew. His list included the injured worker still at the clinic. The cashier almost removed that portion because the man had not completed his delivery shift. The runner insisted the crew order still included him. Yue overheard the correction while stacking empty jars. Rong's contract could hold a foreman painfully responsible for sacks, and his present meal order could still feed a man who was off work.

forest_02_051.speaker: narrator
forest_02_051.text: That afternoon, snow turned to wet needles against the yard windows. The sheltered kitchen smelled stronger of smoke because the cook had reduced its draft. Long Qian came to taste the meal intended for the grain carriers. He complained that the turnips were underdone. The cook pointed to his fuel restriction notice on the wall. He read it, stood still a moment, and ordered more cleared fuel for the shift. The carrier bowls had already been poured.

forest_02_052.speaker: long_qian
forest_02_052.text: 'Keep the notice,' he said when the cook reached to take it down. 'Write the change below it.' She asked whether he wanted the hungry carriers to admire his correction. 'No. I want my clerk to see what the first limit did.' He helped move the waiting bowls closer to the stove. Yue could not decide whether his assistance was courtesy, embarrassment or an effort to remain a tolerable man in a room that knew his signature.

forest_02_053.speaker: narrator
forest_02_053.text: The niece arrived from school carrying a paper horse made with blunt antlers instead of ears. She announced it was a Hart and accused Yue of unfairly looking surprised. Shi Lan inspected the antlers and said they were very good ears for a horse. The child groaned at both adults and put the creature on the bread shelf. Its paper legs spread wider as the room warmed, until the cook gave it a flat tray to stand on.

forest_02_054.speaker: narrator
forest_02_054.text: Over the next two days, the cleared store worked at a smaller pace. The unsafe drying shed stayed shut while the keeper arranged a separate ventilated structure away from lodging. Workers complained about carrying damp sacks farther. The new place was harder to reach and safer to use. Yue helped mark an ordinary dry approach, then carried loads until her last checked ordinary limit. Wen Cai took the next turn when she set one down before her grip began to slip.

forest_02_055.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_055.text: 'I expected a sect apprentice to hide that she was tired,' he said while lifting the replacement load. Yue told him she had tried hiding it often enough to recognize the cost. He asked whether she would teach him the trick of recognizing it sooner. She said they could begin with his left shoulder riding higher than his right. He lowered it, grimaced, and asked how obvious it had been. She made him set the sack down before answering.

forest_02_056.speaker: narrator
forest_02_056.text: The keeper gave them an ordinary handling lesson after the meal break. They practised with an empty frame, then a small checked load, walking to the bench and setting it down without twisting. Wen Cai wanted to race the final return. Yue wanted to win. They both saw the temptation and slowed at the same turn, laughing when the keeper called them perfectly well matched in foolishness. The lesson ended while their movements still remained sound.

forest_02_057.speaker: narrator
forest_02_057.text: On the seventh morning, an eastern delivery count fell short of the buyer's expected bags. The keeper explained the dried yield from the approved billets and the sacks withheld after the accident. Rong Sui compared it against the promise written by the crew foreman. The foreman had guaranteed a dry output before the moisture checks were complete. His own ink now stood between him and his crew. He asked for two more days and refused to meet Yue's eyes.

forest_02_058.speaker: rong_sui
forest_02_058.text: 'I can postpone the cart,' Rong said. 'The household kitchens at the other end will still need fuel on their scheduled day.' Shi Lan asked what quantity could come from his existing town store. He answered with an available figure, lower than the shortfall. 'I will bridge that much. The remainder needs another receiving plan.' He looked at the foreman. 'I am not accepting an unlicensed northern cut as your way to make my arithmetic look right.'

forest_02_059.speaker: narrator
forest_02_059.text: The foreman had expected Rong to welcome any delivered charcoal. His disappointment hardened into anger. After the meeting he called Wen Cai aside and blamed the commission for making every sack slower. Wen answered that the injured worker had not been made slow by an account sheet. Their voices rose. Yue stayed near the store door until the keeper separated the argument into a private work discussion, then asked Wen whether he wanted someone to wait outside.

forest_02_060.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_060.text: 'Yes,' he said after a long hesitation. 'Do not come in and rescue my answer. Just wait.' Yue sat on the low step with a repaired empty sack across her knees. She picked at an old seam while the voices continued behind the door. Waiting felt embarrassingly passive until she remembered that it was the help he had actually asked for. When he came out, he sat beside her and did not begin speaking immediately.

forest_02_061.speaker: narrator
forest_02_061.text: Wen had refused an overnight cut beyond the licensed stand. The foreman threatened to reduce his next turn. Wen's uncle had remained silent. He wanted to tell Yue that he did not care what either man thought; the words would not come out honestly. He cared very much. She let him say that smaller truth, then offered to accompany him to file the disputed work instruction. The choice would remain his after her offer.

forest_02_062.speaker: narrator
forest_02_062.text: They went to Pei Yun before the evening gate closed. The keeper received Wen's account, asked for the actual instruction and named the reply date. She did not promise his family would become less angry. Outside, snow had begun to settle thickly enough to soften the road. Wen stood beneath the lamp and looked toward his uncle's house. Yue watched the same road from beside him, conscious that being free to go back to an apprentice bed was a privilege he did not share.

forest_02_063.speaker: narrator
forest_02_063.text: At supper, Long Qian sent the delayed carrier crew a pot of fully cooked turnips and the revised fuel allowance. Shi Lan's niece tried to persuade Wen's paper Hart to eat one. The legs had dried stiff and held the antlers high. Wen smiled despite himself and cut a tiny paper bowl for it. Yue watched his hands become careful in a gentler way than they were in the store. The forest argument had not won every part of his evening.

forest_02_064.speaker: narrator
forest_02_064.text: On the eighth morning, the injured worker walked from the clinic to his brother's room. He carried nothing. That absence made him look oddly important among people whose arms always contained wood, sacks, bowls, or someone else's parcel. The keeper followed with his bedding. At the threshold, the worker laughed because everyone was watching him perform the magnificent feat of sitting down. Then the laugh became a cough, and the keeper stopped pretending to smile.

forest_02_065.speaker: wen_cai
forest_02_065.text: My uncle says he should have noticed the shutter. He says it while someone else wraps his thumb, while someone else brings his tea, while my sister asks whether he wants the window open. I cannot tell whether he means the shutter or everything. Yesterday I would have liked him to apologize. Today I want him to stop apologizing long enough to tell the doctor which movement hurts. Those wishes turn out to be very different.

forest_02_066.speaker: narrator
forest_02_066.text: The temporary drying rack stood above the millrace, where the wind found it readily and every sack had to be carried uphill. Long Qian offered a covered wagon. Its floor smelled of grain and old onions. The keeper accepted the wagon for transport, inspected its cover, then rejected it as a drying chamber. Long had been preparing to explain how conveniently it could serve both purposes. He swallowed the explanation and fetched another length of rope.

forest_02_067.speaker: long_qian
forest_02_067.text: I know what a wagon costs per day. I do not know what that man would have cost his brother if you had brought him out ten minutes later. The first number keeps presenting itself because it is written in my book. If I sound as though I believe it is the only number, tell me once. I cannot promise to enjoy hearing it, but I would rather be corrected before I order another stupid convenience.

forest_02_068.speaker: narrator
forest_02_068.text: Rong Sui inspected the withheld sacks himself. He wore gloves too fine for the task and ruined one on a broken splinter. Wen expected an accusation. Instead, Rong separated the wet outer pieces from three sacks whose centers were acceptably dry, and asked the keeper to check his selections. Two passed; the third did not. Rong looked at the rejected sack for a while. He left all three where the keeper had put them.

forest_02_069.speaker: rong_sui
forest_02_069.text: My employer would like the shortfall described as delay. The town customer would like it described as theft. Neither has been here. I am going to describe what was ready, what was not, and which order was made before anybody tested the wood. That will offend both sides. Your foreman may find the balance comforting. He should not. His promise is still his promise, and I have not yet decided what remedy to ask for.

forest_02_070.speaker: narrator
forest_02_070.text: That afternoon the foreman brought his own copy of the advance agreement. The paper was greasy at the fold. He had read the eastern delivery clause and the repayment date; a narrow addition on the reverse offered northern cutting as an alternative means of repayment. The addition lacked the land office's approval. He had treated it as assurance that approval would follow. Rong looked away when Wen asked who had first suggested treating it that way.

forest_02_071.speaker: shi_lan
forest_02_071.text: The trees cannot hear an argument about intention. If men cut them tomorrow, we will be left with stumps while everyone argues about what they expected yesterday. I can stop an unauthorized cutting party at the marked line. I cannot erase your flour debt by doing it. Both facts are unpleasant. We had better put them on the same table, because separating them has already made your uncle choose between hunger and a crime he did not understand.

forest_02_072.speaker: narrator
forest_02_072.text: The foreman struck the table with two fingers, a small gesture that managed to sound like a hammer. He had fed twelve workers during the rain, he said. Wen answered that feeding them did not make their signatures appear on his agreement. His uncle closed his eyes. Lin Yue watched a drop of tea creep toward the papers and moved the cup. Nobody thanked her. It was the only helpful thing she could do without taking someone else's answer.

forest_02_073.speaker: rong_sui
forest_02_073.text: The advance was made to the crew business, under the foreman's seal. I will not collect it from Wen Cai's sister or deduct it from the injured man's meal. I will ask the foreman for a revised delivery proposal from licensed stock. I can suspend the disputed northern remedy pending the land office's answer. I cannot forgive the entire advance on my own authority. If you want forgiveness, I will carry the request with the rest of this mess.

forest_02_074.speaker: narrator
forest_02_074.text: When the meeting ended, the uncle stayed behind to pick wet tea leaves from the table's crack. Wen waited in the yard. Lin stood beside him until the cold made waiting feel foolish. Then the uncle came out and asked whether Wen's sister still wanted him to mend her roof frame. Wen said she did, after the doctor cleared his hand. It was not reconciliation. It was a task that would require them to speak again.

forest_02_075.speaker: narrator
forest_02_075.text: The next day brought no snow, only a fierce blue cold. Shi Lan took Lin to the lower ridge to inspect the household wood lots. The cuts there were scattered and modest, each stump older than the charcoal crew's fresh northern marks. A woman carrying brushwood recognized the warden and asked whether the new dispute meant her family had to stop gathering fallen twigs. Shi Lan said no. The woman asked her to say it to the gate clerk too.

forest_02_076.speaker: lin_yue
forest_02_076.text: She believed you while you were standing in front of her. That was not enough to get her past the gate. I used to think a clear answer ended the difficulty. Now I keep finding another person who must hear it, another place where the answer has to survive without its speaker. I suppose that is why I am tired after days when I have done almost nothing that looks like a fight.

forest_02_077.speaker: shi_lan
forest_02_077.text: You climbed three ridges yesterday and carried eighteen sacks the day before. You may also be tired because you have legs. Do not turn every ache into a lesson. Come tomorrow to the gate when the gathering families arrive. You can hear the clerk explain the rule in his own words. Today we still have to look at the north slope, and I would prefer to reach it before the light becomes philosophical.

forest_02_078.speaker: narrator
forest_02_078.text: At the north slope, the snow lay over a skin of ice. A wide hoof had broken through near the path, exposing black water in the depression beneath. There was blood on a snapped reed. Lin crouched, keeping her hands above the print. The animal that had frightened them earlier had crossed here, or another of its kind had. Shi Lan measured the impression and found a smaller track beside it. Their solitary visitor might not have been solitary.

forest_02_079.speaker: narrator
forest_02_079.text: Farther uphill, a broken fence panel leaned against a stump. The fence guarded a cabbage pit, not a charcoal stand. Two cabbages lay crushed outside the opening; the remaining soil cover had collapsed at one corner. An old farmer arrived carrying the salvaged boards. He wanted the beast killed before it returned. Shi Lan asked first whether anyone had been hurt. Nobody had. Then she asked how many cabbages he had lost. He answered immediately: fourteen.

forest_02_080.speaker: shi_lan
forest_02_080.text: Fourteen is enough to matter. I will ask the storehouse about replacement vegetables and have the damaged barrier inspected today. I will also close this narrow approach while we find the animal's passage. Killing it is not a repair for the fence, and chasing it through your cabbage pit could ruin what remains. If it charges people, we will protect them. Right now it has found food beside a route we may have blocked ourselves.

forest_02_081.speaker: narrator
forest_02_081.text: The farmer did not like that answer. He liked the offer of fourteen cabbages well enough to help count the damage again. A neighbor lent boards, with the understanding that the council would replace them if the emergency repair consumed them. Lin and Wen carried the boards uphill. Wen said the Hart had expensive taste. The farmer replied that anything tasted expensive after it had spent six months growing in soil that tried to freeze it.

forest_02_082.speaker: narrator
forest_02_082.text: At dusk, the temporary barrier was finished. It stood clear of the old animal track, keeping people out of the narrow corner while protecting the remaining pit. The farmer tested every brace with his shoulder. Lin stepped back when asked. A few pale hairs clung to the broken fence. Shi Lan put them in a paper fold and marked where they had caught. The physical survey would now have two questions to answer, one about land and one about passage.

forest_02_083.speaker: pei_yun
forest_02_083.text: Bring warm socks tomorrow. The upper stones are not arranged for the convenience of people who prefer straight roads. I will bring the old survey, and the land office will send a measuring assistant. Wen knows the cutting tracks better than I do now. Shi Lan knows where the beast has passed. You know how to listen without grabbing the first answer. We may get somewhere, provided nobody mistakes that list for a reason to leave their lunch behind.

forest_02_084.speaker: narrator
forest_02_084.text: Lin packed bread, dried beans, a spare cloth, and her ordinary practice pages. She left the papers about the kiln in the office, where the people responsible for them could find them. Through the wall she heard Wen's sister laughing at her uncle, who had tried to mend a stool one-handed and made it lean like a drunken crane. Beyond the houses, the ridge lay white and silent. Tomorrow they would discover what its silence had been hiding.
